references.text: God's regret (נִחַמְתִּי) over having created humanity is the direct context and justification for the decision to destroy in verse 7.
Describes the fulfillment of God's judgment announced in 6:7 – all flesh on earth perished in the flood: humans, livestock, creeping things, and birds.
Zephaniah uses almost identical wording: God will wipe out humans and animals, birds and fish from the face of the earth – a clear verbal parallel to Genesis 6:7.
God regrets (נִחַמְתִּי) making Saul king – the same Hebrew expression as in Genesis 6:7 regarding God's regret over creation.
The psalmist prays that sinners should vanish from the earth, reflecting God's decision to remove the wicked from the earth in Genesis 6:7.
God's eschatological judgment on those who destroy the earth reflects the same principle of divine judgment against evil as seen in Genesis 6:7.
Zephaniah's prophecy of future judgment mirrors the structure and scope of the flood's judgment, emphasizing God's righteous action toward all creation at the culmination of sin.
The general judgment in Zephaniah 1:2 is the theological framework for the specific destruction of creatures described in both Zephaniah 1:3 and Genesis 6:7.
Jeremiah uses the image of birds and animals being destroyed as a parallel to the totality of the flood, but here as judgment on a specific group rather than global extinction.
Genesis 1:26 establishes humanity's dominion over creation, while Genesis 6:7 shows how this dominion and creation itself are wiped out because of human sin.
Genesis 7:4 is the direct fulfillment and elaboration of the judgment announced in Genesis 6:7, confirming God's plan to destroy all living things through water.
Jeremiah 27:5 affirms God's sovereignty as Creator, which is the theological basis for His right to destroy creation in Genesis 6:7.
Genesis 7:23 is the direct historical fulfillment of the judgment announced in Genesis 6:7, confirming that the destruction affected all mentioned types of creatures.
